common.previewBanner: Educational prototype — not for clinical use; values pending educator/physicist review
common.disclaimer: Educational simulator — not a diagnostic or clinically validated system. Do not use it for patient care. Technique and tolerance values are provisional demonstration data until reviewed by an educator or medical physicist.

home.title: Practice radiography before the real patient.
home.subtitle: RAD-LAB is an educational simulator for radiologic technology students. Position the patient, set the technique, expose, then learn from precise feedback.
home.provisionalNotice: Technique values in this MVP are provisional demo data and have not been clinically validated. Do not use them as clinical guidance.

workspace.practiceHint: Adjust the patient and equipment so the image meets the request, then press Expose. Detailed feedback is shown afterwards.

console.title: X-ray console
console.subtitle: Educational · vendor-neutral
console.vendorNeutral: Educational, vendor-neutral console — it does not copy any manufacturer's interface. Technique values here are provisional demo values.
console.digitalHint: On a digital system the displayed brightness is processed and is not an exposure meter. After the exposure, technique is judged from the target-relative detector exposure (DI), noise and dose awareness.
console.tubeAngulationHint: Positive = caudad (towards the feet), negative = cephalad. 0° = perpendicular
console.adjustHint: Use − / + or the slider. Arrow keys, Page Up / Page Down, Home and End work on the slider.
console.modeAecHelp: The system ends the exposure from the selected chamber(s). You select kVp and the chambers.
console.masAutoHelp: mAs is set by the AEC in this mode (your manual mAs is kept for when you switch back).

aec.title: AEC sensing chambers
aec.disclaimer: Vendor-neutral educational diagram. Real systems differ in the number, position and shape of chambers, in how they are selected and in how the exposure is terminated.
aec.purpose: AEC aims for consistent, reproducible receptor exposure and compensates for differences in anatomical thickness. Which chambers suit an examination depends on the system and the local protocol.
aec.hint: Select chambers in the diagram or with the checkboxes below. The amber frame is the collimated field.
aec.diagramAlt: Vendor-neutral diagram of the detector with the patient's lung fields, the collimated field and three AEC sensing chambers.

variants.low-exposure: Low detector exposure — increased quantum-noise tendency
variants.excess-exposure: Excess detector exposure — dose-creep risk (may still look acceptable)

result.retryHelp: Retry keeps your last settings so you can correct your mistakes.
result.imageBrightnessNote: Displayed brightness is normalised on digital systems and is not an exposure indicator.
result.scoreNote: An educational score from this simulator, not a real-world accept / reject decision: a radiograph that misses a textbook criterion is not automatically unusable.
result.notDrawn: Scored from your settings — not drawn in this image

result.criticalNote: A critical finding forces “Below the educational pass mark” whatever the numeric score. The numeric score ({total}) and the category weights are unchanged.

technique.title: Technique & exposure analysis
technique.model: Educational model — it does not predict a real detector's exposure index or any patient dose, and its DI bands are provisional.
technique.brightnessTitle: Brightness is not an exposure meter
technique.brightness: On digital radiography, image processing normalises the displayed brightness and contrast, so an image can look acceptable even when detector exposure is too low or too high. Judge exposure by the detector exposure (DI), noise and dose awareness — not by how light or dark the image looks.
technique.gaugeTitle: Detector exposure relative to the target
technique.gaugeAlt: Scale of the deviation index from −6 to +6 with the target at 0 and your exposure marked.
technique.gaugeNote: DI = 10 × log10(EI / EIT). +3 ≈ twice the target exposure, −3 ≈ half. The ±1 and ±3 scoring bands are provisional demo values, not universal limits. EI is not patient dose.

why.kvp: kVp sets the energy spectrum of the beam: it changes penetration and X-ray output. It is not a brightness control — on digital systems processing sets the displayed brightness.
why.mas: With other factors equal, mAs sets how many X-rays are produced. Too little gives too little signal and more quantum noise; more than needed adds radiation without a matching benefit.
why.sid: X-ray intensity falls with the square of the distance (inverse-square law). In manual mode a different SID changes detector exposure: ×{factor} at {sid} cm compared with {ref} cm. The simulator applies only this relationship; a real imaging chain involves more.
why.sidAec: With AEC the model re-terminates at the target, so a different SID changes the mAs the AEC delivers (here {mas} mAs) rather than the detector exposure. SID still changes the geometry (for example magnification).
why.aec: AEC aims for consistent, reproducible receptor exposure. In this model it senses only the selected chambers inside the field, and a chamber under dense anatomy makes it expose for longer. Chamber layout and selection are vendor / local-protocol dependent.
why.di: DI compares detector exposure with a target: 0 = on target, +3 ≈ twice, −3 ≈ half. It is not a patient dose, and there is no universal pass/fail band.
why.noise: Fewer photons reaching the detector mean more quantum noise (noise ∝ 1/√exposure).
why.dose: Digital systems can hide excess exposure behind a good-looking image. The aim is adequate image quality with the least reasonable exposure.

technique.aecBackup: No selected chamber was inside the field: the AEC ran to its backup limit.
technique.assumptionsIntro: Every medical rule behind this feedback is classified. Only “validated” items are claims of fact; the rest are protocol- or demo-specific.

patient.title: Patient instructions
patient.intro: Speak to the patient before the exposure. You choose what to say; the simulated patient then responds to what you said.

breathingOptions.deep-inspiration-hold: “Take a deep breath in and hold it.”

motionOptions.remain-still: “Stay still and don't move until I tell you.”

patient.note: RAD-LAB does not measure real breathing or movement. The result shows an educational consequence of what you said to this simulated patient.

radiograph.title: Simulated educational radiograph
radiograph.alt: Simulated educational PA chest radiograph rendered from your settings; not a diagnostic image.
radiograph.educationalNote: Educational reference appearance — not an image of the case patient, and not a diagnostic or clinically validated radiograph. The visual effects are educational approximations: their size does not measure real rotation, movement, noise or dose.
radiograph.notRepresentative: This projection is not simulated yet. The PA reference appearance is shown for layout only and does not represent your selected projection.
radiograph.failed: The reference image could not be loaded.
radiograph.effectsIntro: Each item links something you did to a visible effect. The clinical concept and the amount drawn are classified separately: the amount drawn is always an educational approximation, never a validated appearance.

baseline.title: Reference appearance
baseline.desc: The reference PA appearance is shown with no simulated faults. It is an educational baseline, not a standard every patient will match.

rotation.title: Rotation → thoracic asymmetry
rotation.desc: The line of the spinous processes moves relative to the medial ends of the clavicles, one hemithorax looks wider than the other and the lungs differ slightly in transradiancy. The direction is supported by the literature; the amount drawn is an educational approximation, not a measurement of degrees of rotation (body build changes this appearance).

collimation-clipping.title: Field edges clip anatomy
collimation-clipping.desc: Anatomy outside the collimated field is not exposed, so it is missing from the image on the side(s) where the field cuts the required region. The field follows your central-ray and collimation settings.

excess-field.title: Larger exposed field
excess-field.desc: A larger field exposes and shows more tissue. No scatter or contrast penalty is drawn, because there is no validated physical model for it here; the real cost is unnecessary exposure.

centering.title: Central ray off-centre → field shifted
centering.desc: The field is centred on your central ray, so a central-ray error moves the exposed area across the anatomy. The anatomy itself stays where it is on the detector.

scapulae.title: Shoulders not rolled forward → scapulae over the lungs
scapulae.desc: Schematic scapulae overlap the lateral lung fields and hide lung tissue. Rolling the shoulders forward moves the scapulae out of the lung fields (a common PA chest quality criterion). The overlay is a schematic, not a real scapula from the reference image.

chin.title: Chin tucked → jaw over the apices
chin.desc: A schematic lower-jaw and soft-tissue shadow overlaps the upper chest and the apices. The chin control is a position cue, not an anatomical angle.

inspiration.title: Reduced inspiration → raised diaphragm
inspiration.desc: After your breathing instruction, the simulated patient did not take a full breath in: the lungs look less expanded, the diaphragm sits higher and the lung fields are shorter. RAD-LAB does not measure real inspiration and uses no rib-count rule.

motion.title: Patient movement → loss of sharpness
motion.desc: Because the stay-still instruction was missing or wrong, the simulated patient moved: edges are blurred. The blur size is an educational approximation, not a movement distance.

low-exposure.title: Low detector exposure → noise
low-exposure.desc: Fewer photons reach the detector, so the image is noisier and subtle low-contrast detail is harder to see. Displayed brightness is kept normalised on purpose: low exposure does not make the image lighter. The noise is a deterministic educational texture, not a prediction for a real detector.

excess-exposure.title: Excess detector exposure → no obvious change
excess-exposure.desc: Detector exposure above the target can still give an acceptable-looking image after digital processing, and the image is not darker. The problem (dose creep) shows in the DI and dose-awareness feedback, not in the picture. More mAs is not rewarded.

low-penetration.title: Low penetration → dense regions less visible
low-penetration.desc: With low kVp, structures behind dense regions (the spine and retrocardiac lung behind the heart, the mediastinum) are less visible. This is separate from detector exposure, and more mAs does not fix it. The change in visibility is an educational approximation, not a measurement.

marker.title: Your side marker
marker.desc: Your marker is drawn where you placed it on the detector and is cut off by the field like any other image content. It is not corrected for you.

projection.title: Projection not simulated
projection.desc: The projection you selected is not simulated in this version. The PA reference appearance is shown for layout only.

radiograph.margins: Dark margins lie outside the collimated field. Grey hatched areas inside the field have no reference-image data: they are not exposure, collimation or anatomy.
radiograph.clippingMarginNote: Margin only at {sides}: the field cuts only the margin of the provisional required region (a demo size awaiting educator review), beyond the lungs, ribs and costophrenic angles drawn in this baseline picture. The score still applies the region, but the picture shows those structures complete.
radiograph.altClippingMargin: At {sides} the field cuts only the margin of the required region; the lungs shown are complete.
radiograph.altReference: No simulated image-quality fault is visible: this is the reference appearance.

baseline.title: Reference appearance
baseline.desc: The reference PA wrist appearance is shown with no simulated faults. It is a teaching approximation: a real normal adult left wrist (a 31-year-old male, as described by its author), not the chest cases' patient. It is not a standard every patient will match.

rotation.title: Rotation → unequal metacarpal spacing, radius and ulna overlap
rotation.desc: In a true PA wrist the spaces between the proximal metacarpals are near-equal, their shafts show equal concavity on both sides, and the distal radius and ulna are separated (Bontrager p.156). With rotation the spaces between the metacarpals become unequal and the ulna and radius move apart or toward each other until they overlap, depending on the direction of the turn. Only the amount of rotation is scored, not its direction. The picture is an educational approximation made from one baseline image with a simple depth model (the turn is drawn exaggerated, about 2.3 times the value), not a measurement of degrees; real carpal movement and the concavity of the shafts are not modelled.

low-penetration.title: Low penetration → less bone detail
low-penetration.desc: With low kVp the dense bones (carpals, bone ends) show less internal detail. This is separate from detector exposure, and more mAs does not fix it. The change in visibility is an educational approximation, not a measurement.

rotation.title: Rotation → bones not superimposed
rotation.desc: In a true lateral wrist the ulnar head lies over the distal radius and the proximal 2nd–5th metacarpals are superimposed (Bontrager p.158). With rotation each of these structures is drawn twice, apart: a stronger copy for the side nearer the detector and a weaker one for the side farther from it. Only the amount of rotation is scored, not its direction. The picture is an educational approximation (two blended copies of whole windows, not structures covering one another) made from one baseline image with a simple depth model (the turn is drawn exaggerated, about 2.3 times the value), not a measurement of degrees.

low-penetration.title: Low penetration → less bone detail

rotation.title: Rotation → unequal spacing of the metacarpals and digits
rotation.desc: In a true PA hand the concavities of the metacarpal shafts and phalanges of digits 2–5 are symmetric and the soft tissue on each side of the phalanges is equal (Bontrager p.150). With rotation the spaces between the shafts and the digits become unequal and the soft tissue on the two sides is no longer equal. Only the amount of rotation is scored, not its direction. The amount drawn is an educational approximation made from one baseline image (a horizontal warp that moves bone and soft tissue together, so the change in concavity itself is not drawn), not a measurement of degrees.

low-penetration.title: Low penetration → less bone detail
low-penetration.desc: With low kVp the dense bones (the carpals and the bone ends) show less internal detail. This is separate from detector exposure, and more mAs does not fix it. The change in visibility is an educational approximation, not a measurement.

baseline.desc: The reference AP (extended) elbow appearance is shown with no simulated faults. It is a teaching approximation: a real normal adult left elbow (a 31-year-old male, as described by its author), not the chest cases' patient. It is not a standard every patient will match.

rotation.title: Rotation → epicondyles not in profile, radial head and ulna apart or superimposed
rotation.desc: In a true AP elbow the epicondyles are in profile and the radial head, neck and tubercle are separated from the ulna or only slightly superimposed by it (Bontrager p.166). With rotation the epicondyles move toward each other (the interepicondylar distance narrows) and the radius is drawn apart from, or over, the ulna. Only the amount of rotation is scored, not its direction. The amount drawn is an educational approximation made from one baseline image (a horizontal warp of the whole arm plus two forearm layers that may overlap, the superimposition drawn as an average), not a measurement of degrees.

low-penetration.title: Low penetration → less bone detail
low-penetration.desc: With low kVp the dense bones (the condyles and the proximal ulna) show less internal detail. This is separate from detector exposure, and more mAs does not fix it. The change in visibility is an educational approximation, not a measurement.

rotation.title: Rotation → condyle outlines not superimposed
rotation.desc: In a true lateral elbow (90° flexion) the epicondyles / condyle outlines are superimposed and about half of the radial head is covered by the coronoid process (Bontrager p.172). With rotation the condyle outlines and the radial head / coronoid region are drawn twice, apart: a stronger copy for the side nearer the detector and a weaker one for the side farther from it. Only the amount of rotation is scored, not its direction. The concentric arcs of the trochlear sulcus and the double ridges of the capitulum and trochlea (other Bontrager criteria) are not drawn: one baseline image cannot show them honestly. The amount drawn is an educational approximation (two blended copies, not a model of structures covering one another), not a measurement of degrees.

low-penetration.title: Low penetration → less bone detail
low-penetration.desc: With low kVp the dense bones (the condyles and the proximal ulna / olecranon) show less internal detail. This is separate from detector exposure, and more mAs does not fix it. The change in visibility is an educational approximation, not a measurement.

rotation.title: Rotation → unequal spacing of metatarsals 2–5
rotation.desc: In a true AP foot the spacing of metatarsals 2–5 is nearly equal; the bases of the 1st and 2nd metatarsals are generally separated and the bases of 2–5 overlap (Bontrager p.232). With rotation the toes and metatarsals shift sideways by different amounts, so the spaces between them become unequal. Only the amount of rotation is scored, not its direction. The amount drawn is an educational approximation made from one baseline image (a horizontal warp of the toes and the metatarsals column by column), not a measurement of degrees.

baseline.title: Reference appearance
baseline.desc: The reference AP medial oblique foot appearance is shown with no simulated faults (the plantar surface within 30°–40°). It is a teaching approximation: a real normal adult right foot, not the chest cases' patient. It is not a standard every patient will match.

rotation.title: Plantar angle → metatarsals 3–5 closer together or further apart
rotation.desc: In a medial oblique foot the plantar surface is 30°–40° to the detector (40° recommended) and metatarsals 3–5 are free of superimposition (Bontrager p.233). As the angle moves away from 40° the toes and metatarsals are drawn displaced sideways by different amounts, so metatarsals 3–5 move closer together or further apart. The amount drawn is an educational approximation made from one baseline image (a horizontal warp of the toes and the metatarsals column by column, taking the picture as 40°), not a measurement of degrees.

low-penetration.title: Low penetration → less bone detail
low-penetration.desc: With low kVp the dense bones (the tarsal bones) show less internal detail. This is separate from detector exposure, and more mAs does not fix it. The change in visibility is an educational approximation, not a measurement.

baseline.title: Reference appearance
baseline.desc: The reference AP knee appearance is shown with no simulated faults. It is a teaching approximation: a real normal adult right knee (a 31-year-old male, per the file description), not the chest cases' patient. It is not a standard every patient will match.

rotation.title: Rotation → condyles asymmetric, fibular head more or less covered
rotation.desc: In a true AP knee the femoral condyles and the joint space are symmetric, about the medial half of the fibular head is superimposed by the tibia and the intercondylar eminence is centred in the fossa (Bontrager p.246). With rotation the condyle edges and the eminence move by different amounts, and the fibula and the tibia move as two layers so the fibular head is covered more or less. Only the amount of rotation is scored, not its direction. The amount drawn is an educational approximation made from one baseline image (a horizontal warp of the whole leg plus two layers below the joint), not a measurement of degrees.

low-penetration.title: Low penetration → less bone detail
low-penetration.desc: With low kVp the dense bones (the femoral condyles and the tibial plateau) show less internal detail. This is separate from detector exposure, and more mAs does not fix it. The change in visibility is an educational approximation, not a measurement.

rotation.title: Rotation → condyle borders not superimposed
rotation.desc: In a true lateral knee the posterior borders of the femoral condyles are superimposed; with over-rotation less of the fibular head is covered by the tibia and with under-rotation more (Bontrager p.249). With rotation the condyle outline and the fibular head region are drawn twice, a far-side copy and a near-side copy, so the outline is doubled. Only the amount of rotation is scored, not its direction. The amount drawn is an educational approximation made from one baseline image (whole windows drawn twice, not occlusion), not a measurement of degrees.

baseline.desc: The reference AP ankle appearance is shown with no simulated faults. It is a teaching approximation: a real adult ankle (a 24-year-old male, per the file description), not the chest cases' patient. It is not a standard every patient will match.

rotation.title: Rotation → mortise spaces change
rotation.desc: In a true AP ankle the medial part of the ankle mortise is open, the lateral part is closed and the distal fibula is partly overlapped by the tibia and the talus (Bontrager p.239). With rotation the columns of the malleoli and the plafond edges move by different amounts, so the clear spaces beside the talus open or close. Only the amount of rotation is scored, not its direction. The amount drawn is an educational approximation made from one baseline image (one smooth horizontal warp of the leg and ankle together; the overlap of the distal fibula is not drawn), not a measurement of degrees.

low-penetration.title: Low penetration → less bone detail
low-penetration.desc: With low kVp the dense bones (the talus and the heel bone) show less internal detail. This is separate from detector exposure, and more mAs does not fix it. The change in visibility is an educational approximation, not a measurement.

rotation.title: Rotation → fibula and joint outlines doubled
rotation.desc: In a true lateral ankle the distal fibula lies over the posterior half of the tibia, the lateral malleolus is seen through the distal tibia and the talus and the tibiotalar joint is open with a uniform space (Bontrager p.242). With rotation the fibula and the joint outline are drawn twice, a far-side copy and a near-side copy, so the outlines are doubled. Only the amount of rotation is scored, not its direction. The amount drawn is an educational approximation made from one baseline image (whole windows drawn twice, not occlusion), not a measurement of degrees.

rotation.desc: The one-image teaching warp makes the iliac/obturator regions asymmetric with pelvic rotation (Bontrager p.279). Independent bone overlaps, hidden trochanters and femoral-neck foreshortening are not reconstructed. This is not a measured or diagnostic projection.

baseline.desc: Reference AP oblique glenoid (Grashey) appearance of a right shoulder from a real radiograph, used as an educational approximation and not clinical ground truth. The source describes recurrent dislocation with no visible abnormality; it is not a normal or asymptomatic shoulder. Your marker is interactive.

rotation.title: Body turn outside 35°–45° → closed joint space
rotation.desc: Outside the 35°–45° body turn (Bontrager p.196) the one-image teaching warp closes the joint space between the humeral head and the glenoid. The glenoid rims, true overlap of the head, the scapular body and arm posture are not reconstructed; the cue is the same for either side of the range. This is not a measured or diagnostic projection.

low-penetration.desc: Low penetration reduces visibility of dense shoulder structures. Magnitudes are educational; brightness is not an exposure indicator.

Leg position is independent; hidden trochanters and femoral-neck foreshortening are not reconstructed on the radiograph. Numeric tolerances and geometry are teaching assumptions.
positioningPelvis.rotationHelp: Rotate the pelvis independently of both legs. Iliac wings and obturator foramina should be symmetric. This one-image warp is a teaching approximation; ±2° full / ±5° partial are engine teaching choices.
positioningPelvis.markerConvention: Marker R inside the field, clear of the anatomy; only the letter is judged. The baseline has no fixed marker. Never mirrored in Arabic.
positioningPelvis.markerHint: Choose R, then place it inside the field and outside the pelvis.

positioningShoulder.schematicNote: Educational schematic, not anatomically exact. The same one-image model closes the joint space in the setup and in the result when the body turn is outside the 35°–45° source range. The arm position is drawn in the setup only and does not change the radiograph; the glenoid rims and head overlap are not reconstructed. Scale, region and tolerances are teaching assumptions.
positioningShoulder.rotationHelp: Turn the body toward the affected (right) shoulder; the angle is the absolute turn from the detector. Bontrager gives 35°–45° and every angle in that range scores the same: there is no single ideal angle. The 30°–50° partial band is an engine teaching choice.
positioningShoulder.markerConvention: Marker R (the patient's right) inside the field, clear of the anatomy; only the letter is judged. The baseline has no fixed marker. Never mirrored in Arabic.
